sections.html:
Hartford is the state capital, on the Connecticut River in Hartford County, with 121,054 residents at the 2020 census packed into about 18 square miles. There is almost no vacant land. Most houses stand on small lots, a large share are multi-family, and buyers tend to judge a property street by street instead of citywide.

Much of the city lies low beside the river, and the record includes floods: in April 1909 the Connecticut River rose to 24.5 feet above low water and covered part of the city, and it flooded again in 1930. If you own near the water, expect buyers and title companies to ask about basements and drainage. Roofs, gutters and heating systems also take a beating through hot, humid summers and snowy winters, so older houses with a worn roof or a damp cellar are common. They still sell: an as-is buyer prices the repairs instead of asking you to make them.

Hartford bills in two installments, July 1 and January 1, and gives a grace date after each one. A last day that lands on a weekend moves to the following Monday. The Tax Collector posts the schedule on its Tax Information page.

InstallmentDueLast day to pay
First installmentJuly 1August 1
Second installmentJanuary 1February 1

After the last day, balances accrue interest at 1.5% per month, which the city restates as 18% per year. Approved elderly applicants follow a different calendar of four installments, due July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. That schedule applies only to applications the city has already approved.

sections.h2: Vehicle, personal property and abatement bills
sections.html:
Personal property and motor vehicle tax follow the same July and January pattern, and any bill over $100 is split into two installments. A vehicle registered after October 2 gets one supplemental bill, due January 1.

The Tax Collector also takes abatement applications. The form has to be fully completed, signed and notarized, and the abatement committee meets quarterly. An incomplete petition is sent back and never reaches the agenda.

  • Pay a vehicle bill early if you need to register a car. The DMV will not register it until the payment clears.
  • Clearance takes about one business day for cash, an in-person card or certified funds, two days for an online card and ten for a check.
  • Keep your receipts. The office lists lost-receipt questions in its own FAQ.

The city's FAQ also has an entry for people who recently bought or sold a Hartford house and want to know what they owe. Call the office for the answer on your parcel.

sections.h2: What happens at a Hartford closing
sections.html:
The title company or closing attorney pays unpaid property tax from the seller's proceeds and records the deed with the city. Because the tax year splits into two installments, a sale in the middle of the year usually leaves one of them partly owed, and that share comes out of the closing statement.

A state filing runs alongside it. The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent submits the conveyance tax return, Form OP-236, to the town clerk when the deed is recorded. It applies to transfers of $2,000 or more unless an exemption fits, and Hartford's town code is 064. The Department of Revenue Services explains the rules on its conveyance tax page.

Two exemptions matter for owners in trouble. One covers a principal residence deeded in lieu of foreclosure. The other covers a principal residence whose price cannot pay the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and other lienable charges ranking ahead of them. Your closing attorney can say whether either one fits.

sections.h2: What to ask the Hartford tax office
sections.html:
Only the office can confirm the balance on a specific account, and an online summary can lag behind a payment you just made. Put these questions to the Tax Collector:

  • What is the total owed today, interest included?
  • Which installments are paid, and what is the next due date?
  • Is a lien recorded on the property, and what does a release require?
  • Does the bill still go to a mortgage company, or to me?

Ask for the answers in writing. Your closing attorney or title company can use them to set the payoff.

sections.h2: Selling a Hartford house with back taxes
sections.html:
Yes, you can. Unpaid tax is normally taken from the sale proceeds at closing, so you do not have to pay it first. The sequence is short: request the payoff, confirm any lien, send the numbers to the title company, and set the closing date after those answers come back.

Hartford sellers often hold inherited or vacant houses, or multi-family buildings with tenants in place. Each adds a step. An estate needs an authorized signer, and a tenant-occupied building needs a plan for access and timing before showings. Because buyers care more about the building's condition than its address, a house that needs work is often easier to sell as-is than to repair and list.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Hartford houses as-is, including those with back taxes, and the title company settles what is owed from the proceeds.

faqs.q: When are Hartford property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax is due July 1 and January 1. The city lists August 1 and February 1 as the last days to pay, moved to Monday when those dates fall on a weekend.

faqs.q: What interest does Hartford charge on late real estate tax?
faqs.a: Delinquent balances accrue interest at 1.5% per month, or 18% per year.

faqs.q: Is there a different payment plan for elderly Hartford owners?
faqs.a: Yes, for approved applications only. Payment is in four installments due July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Hartford house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax is normally paid from the proceeds at closing. Get a payoff from the tax office and have your title company confirm it.

faqs.q: Who files the Connecticut conveyance tax return?
faqs.a: The seller, the seller's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded.
